column5: heard good news; did not benefit
column6: The commentary makes the reminder's benefit conditional on what happens within its hearer; Hebrews says the preached message did not benefit those who heard because it was not joined with faith, naming the inward response the Qur'anic condition leaves unstated.

column5: hearer forgets the mirror
column6: The commentary contrasts a reminder retained with one avoided; James depicts a hearer who looks and immediately forgets, making forgetfulness the failure to carry a received word forward.

column5: persevering doer is blessed
column6: The commentary says reminder's benefit lies in its destination, purification and prayer; James says the one who perseveres in the law and acts is blessed, specifying action as the benefit's fruit.

column5: word held in a good heart
column6: The commentary's water-skin image says reminder helps when held, and its next verses distinguish recipients; Luke's good soil hears, holds the word in a good heart, and bears fruit with endurance.

column5: hearing, accepting, fruit
column6: The commentary places benefit in the hearer's response rather than the messenger's control; Mark's good soil hears and accepts the word and yields thirty-, sixty-, or hundredfold fruit.

column5: understands and bears fruit
column6: The commentary says the one who fears remembers while another avoids the reminder; Matthew's good soil hears and understands the word and bears fruit, giving a concrete Gospel account of receptive benefit.

column5: word accomplishes its purpose
column6: The commentary likens useful reminder to water that remains after flood foam passes; Isaiah says rain makes earth sprout and God's sent word accomplishes what he intends, joining divine speech to effective growth.

column5: rain waters and makes seed grow
column6: The commentary links benefit with what water leaves behind; Isaiah describes rain and snow watering earth, making it bring forth and sprout, a specific image for speech that nourishes rather than vanishes.

column5: Torah meditated day and night
column6: The commentary says remembrance begins by holding a word in mind; Psalm 1's blessed person meditates on the LORD's instruction day and night, grounding lasting fruit in sustained attention to scripture.

column5: tree by streams, fruit and unfading leaf
column6: The commentary reads benefit as what remains after flood foam goes; Psalm 1 pictures a fruitful tree beside water whose leaf does not wither, a sharply specific image of retained, life-giving sustenance.

column5: remember Moses' Torah at Horeb
column6: The commentary labels ayah 87:9 with Arabic ذ ك ر; Hebrew זכר is its Semitic cognate. WLC Malachi 3:22 commands remembering Moses' law from Horeb, tying the reminder to the named pages of Moses.

column5: book of remembrance; those who fear and honor the name
column6: The commentary's Arabic root label ذ ك ر has the Hebrew cognate זכר; Malachi describes a remembrance book for those who fear the LORD and esteem his name, closely meeting 87:10's fearer and 87:15's remembered name.

column5: remember former generations; ask elders
column6: The commentary labels ذ ك ر as remembering what has passed and links 87:9 to earlier scripture; Hebrew זכר is cognate, and Moses tells Israel to remember ancient days and ask parents and elders.

column5: keep what the eyes saw in the heart; teach descendants
column6: The commentary labels the Arabic root ذ ك ر as holding memory and says reminder passes from messenger to others; Hebrew זכר is cognate, while Moses commands keeping Horeb's witnessed events in the heart and teaching children and grandchildren.

column5: remember the exodus across generations
column6: The commentary labels Arabic ذ ك ر and connects reminder to old pages; Hebrew זכר is cognate, and Moses makes the departure from Egypt something Israel must remember as a recurring account.

column5: God's name as memorial through generations
column6: The commentary joins remembrance to the Lord's name and to earlier pages; Arabic ذ ك ر and Hebrew זכר are cognates, and Exodus calls the divine name a memorial for every generation.

column5: remember the giver of prosperity
column6: The commentary says benefit is a means whose source is God, not self-interest; Arabic ذ ك ر and Hebrew זכר are cognates, and Deuteronomy commands Israel to remember the LORD who gives power to make wealth.

column5: teach the words through daily life
column6: The commentary says the messenger's received word passes to others; Deuteronomy commands parents to teach God's words to children and speak them at home, on the road, at bedtime, and on rising.

column5: visible tassels prompt remembering and doing
column6: The commentary says a reminder must be retained rather than passed by; Numbers gives Israel a visible fringe as a cue to remember the commandments and do them instead of following heart and eyes.

column5: Torah scroll kept as witness
column6: The commentary says the current reminder also points to earlier written pages; Moses orders the Torah scroll placed beside the ark as a witness against Israel, making scripture itself a preserved testimony.

column5: manna kept before the testimony
column6: The commentary develops the reminder as something held in a container; Exodus preserves a jar of manna before the testimony for future generations, turning a material provision into a retained witness.

column5: reading Jeremiah prompts prayer
column6: The commentary says what is recalled is both visible creation and a prior word; Daniel reads Jeremiah's written prophecy, understands its years, then turns toward God in prayer, showing old scripture becoming present supplication.

column5: public reading explained so people understand
column6: The commentary moves from recitation to a hearer's own remembrance; Nehemiah's readers explain the Torah so the assembled people understand, a concrete model of scripture made intelligible to its audience.

column5: listeners rejoice after understanding the reading
column6: The commentary says a reminder reaches its end when the listener receives it; Nehemiah says the people celebrate because they understood the words read to them, showing a response beyond mere hearing.

column5: scroll read so hearers may turn
column6: The commentary's “if the reminder benefits” leaves the hearer's response open; Jeremiah's scroll is written so Judah may hear calamity, turn from evil, and be forgiven, making the hoped-for benefit explicit.

column5: hearing without fear or repentance
column6: The commentary distinguishes a listener who remembers from one who turns away; Judah's leaders hear the scroll but are not afraid or moved to tear their clothes, an exact scene of reminder that fails to benefit.

column5: burned scroll rewritten
column6: The commentary links present reminder to words preserved in earlier pages; after Jehoiakim burns the scroll, Jeremiah dictates it again with many similar words, showing the message survives rejection.

column5: God awakens the ear; servant sustains the weary with speech
column6: The commentary begins with a messenger taught and preserved before he reminds others; Isaiah's servant receives a daily listening ear and a trained tongue to sustain the weary, a close pattern of reception becoming proclamation.

column5: look back to Abraham and Sarah
column6: The commentary says 87:18-19 identifies Abraham's and Moses' pages as the prior word being recalled; Isaiah explicitly tells its hearers to look to Abraham and Sarah as the source of their people and hope.

column5: God teaches for benefit and leads the way
column6: The commentary calls benefit a means that guides toward good; Isaiah says the LORD teaches what is for Israel's profit and leads them in the way they should go, a direct scriptural formulation of reminder as guidance.

column5: do not forget God's benefits
column6: The commentary's ayah links reminder with benefit; Psalm 103 commands blessing the LORD and not forgetting all his benefactions, making memory the answer to received good.

column5: wondrous acts made memorable
column6: The commentary presents creation and past revelation as what reminder brings back; Psalm 111 says the LORD's wondrous works are made to be remembered and joins that memory to divine grace and compassion.

column5: claim that serving God brings no profit
column6: The commentary asks whether reminder benefits and contrasts lasting good with passing gain; Malachi records people asking what profit there is in keeping God's charge, then distinguishes those who fear him in 3:16.

column5: rebuke the neighbor rather than bear sin
column6: The commentary's Sabbath-village admonishers explain that they warn as an answer before God and perhaps to prevent sin; Leviticus commands reproof of one's neighbor, linking correction with the admonisher's responsibility.

column5: Nineveh believes the warning and fasts
column6: The commentary distinguishes those who take reminder from those who avoid it; Jonah's city hears a threatened judgment, believes God, and responds with fasting, a specific case where warning benefits its audience.

column5: watchman warns even if the wicked does not turn
column6: The commentary says the preacher is not responsible for another's refusal and can still benefit by warning; Ezekiel's watchman is delivered if he warns, even when the wicked refuses to turn, specifying the warning duty and its limit.

column5: Wisdom invites hearers to turn at reproof
column6: The commentary says no audience should be judged in advance because its response is hidden; Proverbs portrays Wisdom publicly offering reproof and promising to pour out her teaching to those who turn.

column5: Wisdom's call refused
column6: The commentary's “most wretched” avoids the reminder; Proverbs personifies Wisdom saying that those she called refused and ignored her outstretched hand, a concrete rejected invitation with consequences in the surrounding scene.

column5: hearer dwells secure
column6: The commentary associates reminder with the fearer and successful guidance; Proverbs contrasts the refuser with one who listens to Wisdom and lives securely without fear of disaster.

column5: soft answer turns away anger
column6: The commentary cites a gentle word to Pharaoh as a reminder whose outcome cannot be forced; Proverbs says a soft answer turns away wrath, giving a wisdom-text account of the speech's possible effect.

column5: patient speech can persuade a ruler
column6: The commentary's Moses and Aaron are told to address Pharaoh gently despite his defiance; Proverbs says patience can persuade a ruler and a soft tongue can break resistance, a precise royal-audience parallel.

column5: Sabbath breaker gathers sticks, unlike the Qur'anic fishing town
column6: The commentary recounts a whole coastal community violating Sabbath fishing rules and separates admonishers from offenders; Numbers instead presents one man gathering sticks and a death sentence, making the changed scene and communal response salient.

column5: Sabbath commanded as a memorial practice
column6: The commentary's saved admonishers speak to a town violating Sabbath; Exodus begins the Sabbath command with a call to remember, giving the shared weekly setting a scriptural memory practice.

column5: Baal's prophets call without an answer
column6: The commentary's Abraham asks whether idols can hear those who invoke them; Elijah's scene has Baal's prophets cry out all morning without any voice or answer, dramatizing the test of an unresponsive deity.

column5: idols have ears but cannot hear
column6: The commentary's Abraham asks whether the idols hear their worshipers; Psalm 115 says manufactured gods have ears but do not hear, supplying a direct Israelite statement of the same inability.

column5: idols cannot act with their hands or feet
column6: The commentary asks if idols benefit or harm their worshipers; Psalm 115 says they cannot handle, walk, or make a sound, describing the inert objects behind that question.

column5: idols cannot speak, walk, or do good or harm
column6: The commentary quotes Abraham's test of whether idols benefit or harm; Jeremiah describes idols as carried objects unable to speak or walk and unable to do good or evil, almost the same test in prophetic satire.

column5: challenge to idols to do good or harm
column6: The commentary uses Abraham's question about idols' benefit and harm; Isaiah challenges rival gods to do good or bad so their power can be seen, turning the same criterion into a public test.

column5: petitioning an idol for health, life, or help
column6: The commentary says Abraham exposes people trusting what cannot benefit them; Wisdom describes a craftsman asking a lifeless image for health, life, and assistance, making the misplaced expectation concrete.

column5: wealth cannot deliver in wrath's day
column6: The commentary says worldly goods do not benefit on the final day; Proverbs says riches are useless on the day of wrath while righteousness delivers from death, a precise valuation of benefit under judgment.

column5: Moses' staff designated for signs
column6: The commentary notes that Musa's ordinary staff becomes a sign; Exodus tells Moses to take the staff in his hand because he will perform signs with it, supplying the Hebrew-scriptural scene without implying a shared root for “benefit.”

column5: Aaron's staff preserved as warning-sign
column6: The commentary joins a useful staff to a message that must be retained; Numbers orders Aaron's rod kept before the testimony as a sign against rebels, a physical object preserved to remind and restrain.

column5: staff brings water from the rock
column6: The commentary links the staff's practical use with water that sustains and with its becoming a divine sign; Exodus has Moses strike the rock with his staff and water flow for the people.

column5: forgetting a word of Torah treated as grave loss
column6: The commentary describes Arabic root ذ ك ر as keeping something in mind; Avot reads Deuteronomy.s distinct warning against forgetting as a grave duty to retain even one Torah teaching, adding a strict rabbinic consequence to the biblical exhortation.

column5: Passover story re-enacted in every generation
column6: The commentary connects the reminder to the earlier pages about Moses; the Mishnah makes each generation tell the Exodus as its own deliverance, showing scripture's memory carried through a recurring meal.

column5: rebuke required even repeatedly
column6: The commentary's admonishers warn despite doubt that offenders will benefit; the Talmud derives from Leviticus 19:17 that one must rebuke a fellow and even repeat it, interpreting reproof as a duty rather than a guaranteed result.

column5: ancestors kept alive by public praise
column6: The commentary ends by naming Abraham's and Moses' pages as earlier revelation; Sirach begins its ancestral praise with fathers of old, presenting remembered forebears as instruction for later readers.

column5: Abraham remembered as covenant keeper
column6: The commentary says Abraham's pages carry the reminder into prior scripture; Sirach describes Abraham as great father who kept the Most High's law and entered covenant, showing what Jewish recollection draws from his story.

column5: Moses' memory blessed among people
column6: The commentary names Moses' pages as an earlier source of the reminder; Sirach's praise of Moses describes him as beloved by God and people, a Jewish retelling of Moses as enduring remembered witness.

column5: hears Jesus' words and does them
column6: The commentary says the reminder helps when it is held and acted on; Matthew's wise builder hears Jesus' words and does them, beginning the contrast between received speech that lasts and speech left unused.

column5: flood tests the house that stands
column6: The commentary links benefit with water that remains after a flood; Matthew's storm and flood strike the house founded on rock but do not make it fall, illustrating durable outcome from obeyed words.

column5: hears but does not do
column6: The commentary distinguishes the one who takes reminder from the one who avoids it; Matthew's foolish builder hears Jesus' words but does not do them, making failed reception explicit.

column5: flood exposes the fallen house
column6: The commentary contrasts lasting benefit with what passes away; Matthew's rain and floods wash away the house of the hearer who did not act, a contrary outcome to the enduring house in 7:25.

column5: Moses and the prophets are available witnesses
column6: The commentary says the reminder is both a present word and an earlier scripture; Abraham answers the rich man's request to warn his brothers by pointing them to Moses and the prophets already available to hear.

column5: refusal persists even after a resurrection sign
column6: The commentary leaves benefit conditional on the listener; Abraham says those who do not hear Moses and the prophets will not be persuaded even if someone rises from the dead, a severe account of refusal's limit.

column5: Spirit reminds disciples of Jesus' words
column6: The commentary traces how a received word is retained before being passed to others; Jesus says the Spirit will remind disciples of everything he told them, locating memory within the hearer's life.

column5: women remember Jesus' earlier words
column6: The commentary describes memory as retrieving what had escaped the mind; Luke says the women remember Jesus' prediction after the empty tomb, a precise return of prior speech to mind.

column5: disciples see signs yet fail to remember provision
column6: The commentary contrasts visible signs with the hidden question of whether people retain their meaning; Jesus asks disciples who have eyes and ears whether they still do not remember the loaves, exposing failure to learn from witnessed provision.

column5: disciples remember Jesus' words after resurrection
column6: The commentary links present reminder to earlier pages and later recognition; John says the disciples remembered Jesus' saying after he was raised and then believed scripture and his word.

column5: earlier writings give endurance, comfort, and hope
column6: The commentary says old scriptures supply the content of present reminder; Paul says what was written before was written for instruction, so readers may have endurance and hope.

column5: Israel's past written as warning for later readers
column6: The commentary presents remembered revelation as a warning to those who now hear; Paul says wilderness events were written as examples and admonition for the ends of the ages.

column5: sacred writings make wise for salvation
column6: The commentary calls the reminder a means leading to good and connects it to earlier pages; Timothy has known sacred writings from childhood, which are able to make him wise for salvation.

column5: Scripture useful for teaching and correction
column6: The commentary defines reminder as a means that leads toward good; Paul says scripture is useful for teaching, reproof, correction, and training, detailing the benefit that a received text can provide.

column5: apostolic letter stirs memory
column6: The commentary describes reminder as bringing back what has slipped away; Peter says he writes to stir his readers' sincere minds by way of reminder.

column5: remember prophets and apostolic command
column6: The commentary joins the current reminder with older pages; Peter directs readers to remember the words spoken beforehand by holy prophets and the Lord's command through apostles.

column5: reminder despite already knowing
column6: The commentary says reminder retrieves what the audience may already have heard rather than teaching only something new; Peter plans to remind believers even though they know and are established in the truth.

column5: record remains after teacher's departure
column6: The commentary links a messenger's reminder to enduring earlier pages; Peter makes provision so that after his death readers can recall these things, turning oral instruction into lasting memory.

column5: daily mutual exhortation against hardening
column6: The commentary separates the fearer who remembers from the one who avoids the reminder; Hebrews applies Psalm 95's “today” to daily mutual exhortation so sin's deceit will not harden anyone.

column5: God, not the messenger, gives growth
column6: The commentary says reminder's benefit is not controlled by its speaker; Paul says the planter and waterer are nothing and God gives the growth, making the hidden source of efficacy explicit.

column5: one message, perishing and saved hearers
column6: The commentary leaves open whether reminder benefits and describes opposite recipients; Paul says the message of the cross is folly to those perishing but God's power to those being saved.

column5: message written on hearts
column6: The commentary's vessel image says a reminder benefits when retained within its hearer; Paul describes the community as Christ's letter written not on stone but on human hearts.

column5: gentle correction may lead to repentance
column6: The commentary says Moses and Aaron must speak gently to Pharaoh without presuming the result; Paul requires correction of opponents with gentleness, since God may grant them repentance.

column5: eucharistic bread as remembrance
column6: The commentary says reminder culminates in the hearer's own recollection and worship; Paul reports Jesus' instruction to eat the bread in remembrance of him, making memory a repeated communal act.

column5: cup repeated in remembrance
column6: The commentary joins remembrance with prayer and worship; Paul says the cup is taken as often as believers drink it in remembrance of Jesus, a recurring ritual form of recall.

column5: meal commanded as a memorial
column6: The commentary says a received reminder becomes the listener's own act of remembrance; Jesus commands the disciples to repeat the bread-breaking in his memory, grounding recall in shared worship.

column5: enduring word is the good news preached
column6: The commentary contrasts fading pasture with a reminder carried from earlier pages; Peter quotes Isaiah that the Lord's word remains forever and identifies it as the good news preached to his readers.

column5: God discloses hidden purposes of hearts
column6: The commentary says whether reminder takes hold is hidden from the messenger but known to God; Paul says the Lord will bring hidden things to light and disclose heart's purposes.

column5: remember what was received and heard
column6: The commentary defines reminder as recovering what slipped away and responding to it; Revelation tells its hearers to remember what they received and heard, keep it, and repent.

column5: words on heart and body as signs
column6: The commentary says reminder must be held rather than let pass; Deuteronomy places God's words on heart and soul and binds them on hand and forehead, making bodily signs a memory aid.

column5: word stored in the heart
column6: The commentary describes zikir as keeping a word in mind; the psalmist says he has stored God's word in his heart so he will not sin, a direct image of retained reminder shaping conduct.

column5: words kept within the heart
column6: The commentary's vessel image says reminder benefits when retained inside its hearer; Proverbs tells the learner not to let wisdom's words leave the eyes but to keep them within the heart.

column5: wisdom's words are life and healing
column6: The commentary says benefit is the good reached through reminder; Proverbs says the words found by the learner are life and healing, specifying the effect of holding instruction.

column5: word dwelling richly, teaching and singing
column6: The commentary says reminder can become the hearer's own words and worship; Paul says Christ's word should dwell richly as believers teach and admonish one another with psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs.

column5: hear message, examine scriptures daily
column6: The commentary connects present reminder with earlier pages; the Bereans receive Paul's message eagerly and examine the scriptures day by day to see whether it is so, showing hearers actively testing proclamation against prior writings.

column5: rod and staff comfort the traveler
column6: The commentary says a staff is both a practical support and a possible sign; Psalm 23's shepherd uses rod and staff to comfort a traveler in danger, giving the tool a protective role.

column5: repent one day before death
column6: The commentary sets timely reminder against the person who remembers only when judgment arrives; Rabbi Eliezer's teaching says to repent one day before death, and the disciples' question makes the need to act now explicit.

column5: patient preaching, correction, and exhortation
column6: The commentary says the messenger is to remind without controlling the audience; Paul charges Timothy to preach, reprove, rebuke, and exhort with patience and teaching.

column5: remember the word-teacher night and day
column6: The commentary traces revelation received by a messenger and carried into the hearer; the Didache instructs a disciple to remember the one speaking God's word night and day, then honor him.

column5: scripture reading followed by exhortation and prayer
column6: The commentary moves from reminder to the listener's worshipful response; Justin describes Sunday readings from prophets and apostolic memoirs followed by the leader's instruction and common prayer.

column5: memorial written and recited to Joshua
column6: The commentary labels the Arabic source root ذ ك ر as holding and recalling a word; Exodus uses Hebrew זכר in ordering a written memorial and its recitation into Joshua's hearing, joining cognate wording to preserved proclamation.

column5: tell the next generation God's acts
column6: The commentary says the present reminder points back to prior revelation; the psalmist refuses to hide the LORD's praise, strength, and wonders from children, making intergenerational retelling the means of memory.

column5: future children must tell their children
column6: The commentary traces a received word from messenger to later hearer; Psalm 78 says a generation yet unborn should know the works and tell its own children, extending the chain beyond the first audience.

column5: hope in God and not forget his works
column6: The commentary contrasts the one who remembers with the one who avoids the reminder; this psalm warns later generations not to become stubborn like their ancestors, but to hope in God and remember his works.

column5: rebellious generation refuses its inherited trust
column6: The commentary's wicked hearer turns away from a reminder; Psalm 78 describes ancestors as stubborn and unfaithful, showing how inherited instruction can fail to produce a faithful response.

column5: Israel forgot the signs of the exodus
column6: The commentary defines remembrance against forgetting and recalls God's visible acts; Psalm 78 says Israel did not remember the divine power and signs that freed them from Egypt, a concrete failure to learn from provision.

column5: remember wonders and judgments
column6: The commentary's Arabic root label ذ ك ر concerns remembering and connects reminder to past revelation; Psalm 105 uses Hebrew זכר for remembering God's wonders and judgments, then recounts the ancestral story.

column5: call on the name and make God's deeds known
column6: The commentary says reminder ends with the hearer remembering the Lord's name and praying; Psalm 105 joins calling on God's name with making his deeds known among peoples.

column5: remember the wilderness testing of the heart
column6: The commentary says God knows what is public and hidden and asks what the reminder brings back; Moses says Israel must remember the wilderness journey where God humbled and tested what was in the heart.

column5: ritual confession of rescue from Egypt
column6: The commentary links the present reminder to earlier pages and to God's provision; Israel's firstfruits confession recounts the LORD's rescue from Egypt, making memory part of gratitude for the land's harvest.

column5: covenant book read aloud and accepted
column6: The commentary says a messenger's reminder should be received and acted on; Moses reads the covenant book to the people, who answer that they will do and obey what the LORD said.

column5: Josiah hears the book and recognizes neglected obedience
column6: The commentary connects remembered scripture with accountability; after the book is read, Josiah asks about the wrath due because their ancestors did not obey its words, showing a text's benefit as moral awakening.

column5: covenant book read to all the people
column6: The commentary says earlier pages are the content of the current reminder; Josiah reads the covenant book before Judah's elders and all the people, making the written word a public call to renewal.

column5: receive words in heart and ears before speaking
column6: The commentary says the messenger first retains what was given, then passes it to others; Ezekiel is told to take God's words into his heart and hear them with his ears before going to the exiles.

column5: whether they hear or refuse, they will know a prophet came
column6: The commentary says the reminder's benefit is hidden and the messenger does not control the response; Ezekiel is sent to a rebellious house and must speak even if they refuse, while the encounter itself remains a testimony.

column5: speak the words whether heard or refused
column6: The commentary's imperative to remind does not let the speaker dictate reception; Ezekiel must speak God's words to the rebellious house whether they listen or not, clarifying the prophetic duty beside the Qur'anic condition.

column5: address exiles even if they refuse to hear
column6: The commentary says the reminder is offered while its effect belongs to the hearer; Ezekiel must go to the exiles and speak God's words whether they hear or refuse, repeating the duty across the prophet's commission.

column5: God teaches Moses what to say
column6: The commentary begins with God teaching the messenger before commanding him to remind others; God promises to be with Moses' mouth and teach him what to say, a direct pattern of received speech becoming proclamation.

column5: speak whatever God commands without fear
column6: The commentary moves from the messenger's preservation to his task of reminding people; Jeremiah is told to go where God sends him and speak what he commands, not to fear the audience.

column5: God puts his words in the prophet's mouth
column6: The commentary says the messenger first receives a word and then transfers it to others; Jeremiah's mouth is touched and God's words are placed there, closely paralleling the received-proclamation sequence.

column5: prophet speaks the words God puts in his mouth
column6: The commentary links divine teaching of the messenger to later reminder; God promises to raise a prophet like Moses, put words in his mouth, and require him to speak what God commands.

column5: humble person trembles at God's word
column6: The commentary says the one who fears is the hearer who remembers; Isaiah says God regards the poor and contrite person who trembles at his word, specifying a receptive posture rather than status.

column5: the heavens declare God's glory
column6: The commentary says reminder recalls what is visible to everyone in creation; the psalm calls the heavens a public declaration of God's glory, a nonverbal witness alongside the earlier written word.

column5: God sees the heart, not outward appearance
column6: The commentary warns against judging the blind seeker by appearance or favoring the self-satisfied prominent man; in choosing David, God tells Samuel that people see appearance but the LORD sees the heart.

column5: Abraham teaches his household God's way
column6: The commentary names Abraham's pages as a prior reminder; Genesis says Abraham will command his children and household after him to keep the LORD's way, joining his remembered story to teaching descendants.

column5: remember rescue when keeping Sabbath
column6: The commentary's Sabbath-town scene turns on a command people violate and admonishers defend; Deuteronomy grounds Sabbath observance in remembering Israel's rescue from slavery, adding the deliverance memory behind the weekly command.

column5: Moses' staff parts the sea
column6: The commentary traces Moses' ordinary staff becoming a divine sign; Exodus commands Moses to lift the staff over the sea, where it becomes the instrument of deliverance through water.

column5: a raised sign lets the bitten live
column6: The commentary says Moses' useful staff can become a sign that points beyond itself; Numbers has Moses raise a serpent so the bitten who look toward it live, a parallel of an object turned into a sign of benefit.

column5: serpent sign recalls the law's command
column6: The commentary's staff discussion distinguishes an ordinary object from its signifying role; Wisdom interprets the wilderness serpent as a sign of salvation that reminds Israel of God's law, giving the sign a memory function.

column5: salvation comes from God, not the object seen
column6: The commentary says Moses' staff may point to the Lord rather than derive power from its practical use; Wisdom says the healed person was saved not by the visible thing but by God, explicitly interpreting the sign's source.

column5: tree by water keeps fruiting in drought
column6: The commentary says useful reminder is what remains and bears good after a flood; Jeremiah's trusting person is like a tree by water whose leaves stay green and whose fruit does not cease in heat.

column5: river water yields fruit and healing leaves
column6: The commentary develops water that benefits and remains; Ezekiel's river feeds trees bearing monthly fruit, whose leaves heal, making life-giving water a sustained outcome rather than passing foam.

column5: silver and gold cannot deliver in judgment
column6: The commentary says worldly wealth cannot benefit on the day that matters; Zephaniah says silver and gold will not rescue people on the LORD's day of wrath, specifying the limit of material benefit.

column5: wealth does not accompany a person in death
column6: The commentary contrasts fleeting worldly life with the more enduring hereafter; Psalm 49 says a person carries nothing away at death, exposing the limit of possessions as benefit beyond life.

column5: God repeatedly sends messengers out of compassion
column6: The commentary's Sabbath admonishers warn as a duty even when benefit is uncertain; Chronicles says God sends messengers repeatedly because he has compassion for his people, grounding warning in mercy.

column5: mocked messengers, no remedy remains
column6: The commentary distinguishes the people who receive a reminder from those who reject it; Chronicles says the people mocked God's messengers until wrath rose and there was no remedy, a severe account of refusal's end.

column5: Wisdom is called after being rejected, but does not answer
column6: The commentary says reminder can be refused and judgment may arrive after its useful time; Proverbs portrays rejected Wisdom as unavailable when her former hearers later call in distress.

column5: rejection rooted in refusing fear and knowledge
column6: The commentary says the fearer remembers while the wicked avoids the reminder; Proverbs names the refusers' choice as hating knowledge and not choosing fear of the LORD.

column5: Torah transmitted from Moses through generations
column6: The commentary links present reminder to the pages of Moses and Abraham; Avot opens by tracing Torah's reception at Sinai and its transmission through Joshua, elders, prophets, and later teachers.

column5: failure to protest extends responsibility to a community
column6: The commentary's Sabbath admonishers ask why warn a town and answer that they must answer to God; the Talmud extends the duty to protest from one's household to one's town and the wider community.

column5: pay close attention lest the heard message drift away
column6: The commentary describes zikir as holding what might otherwise be lost; Hebrews urges hearers to attend more closely to what they heard so they do not drift from it.

column5: remind readers who already know, using the exodus warning
column6: The commentary says reminding can retrieve known truth rather than introduce a novelty; Jude explicitly reminds readers who already know of Israel's rescue from Egypt and the later destruction of those who did not believe.

column5: remember Jesus raised from the dead
column6: The commentary traces remembrance from messenger to hearer and ties it to the pages of Abraham and Moses; Paul commands Timothy to remember the risen Jesus as the center of the gospel he preaches.

column5: Timothy sent to remind the community of Paul's teaching
column6: The commentary describes the messenger's task as reminding listeners of received teaching; Paul says he sent Timothy to remind the Corinthians of his ways in Christ, which he teaches everywhere.

column5: Paul writes boldly as a reminder by grace
column6: The commentary says reminder is a messenger's task grounded in what was given; Paul explains that he wrote boldly to remind the Roman believers because of the grace given to him.

column5: remember Jesus' saying to help the weak
column6: The commentary distinguishes Arabic benefit from self-serving profit and describes benefit as helping others; Paul tells elders to work and help the weak, remembering Jesus' saying that giving is more blessed than receiving.

column5: seek another person's good
column6: The commentary says the Arabic idea of benefit faces outward toward people rather than private gain; Paul tells believers not to seek their own good but the good of another, a direct ethical counterpart.

column5: bring a wanderer back from error
column6: The commentary says reminder retrieves what has slipped away and may lead to salvation; James describes a believer turning someone who has wandered from the truth back again.

column5: saving a sinner from death
column6: The commentary defines reminder's benefit by where it leads; James says the one who turns a sinner from error saves that person's soul from death, stating the stakes of successful correction.

column5: disciples later remember words written about Jesus
column6: The commentary joins present reminder to earlier pages; John says the disciples did not understand at first, but after Jesus was glorified they remembered what had been written and done.

column5: God helps Israel by remembering mercy
column6: The commentary links the reminder to Abraham's and Moses' pages and to the fearer's salvation; Mary's song says God helps Israel by remembering mercy, interpreting the present rescue through covenant memory.

column5: mercy spoken to Abraham and his descendants
column6: The commentary says 87:18-19 places the current reminder in Abraham's earlier pages; Mary's song says this mercy is what God spoke to the ancestors, to Abraham and his offspring.

column5: remember the covenant made with the fathers
column6: The commentary calls remembrance a return to earlier revelation; Zechariah's song says God shows mercy to the fathers and remembers his holy covenant.

column5: rain and fruitful seasons witness to God
column6: The commentary says visible creation and provision are reminders; Paul says God did not leave himself without witness, giving rain, fruitful seasons, food, and gladness.

column5: creation makes God's unseen power perceptible
column6: The commentary says the reminder can be what everyone sees in the created world; Paul says God's invisible qualities are understood through what has been made, leaving people without excuse.

column5: God's kindness leads toward repentance
column6: The commentary says reminder's benefit is its movement toward purification and good; Paul says God's kindness, patience, and forbearance are meant to lead a person to repentance.

column5: hardness stores up judgment
column6: The commentary contrasts the hearer who receives reminder with one who avoids it; Paul says a hard and unrepentant heart stores up wrath, spelling out the consequence of refusing repentance.

column5: one proclamation has life and death outcomes
column6: The commentary says the reminder may benefit one hearer and not another; Paul describes the same ministry as an aroma from death to death for some and from life to life for others.

column5: worldly gain may cost the soul
column6: The commentary says benefit must be measured by the lasting good rather than worldly life; Jesus asks what a person gains by acquiring the whole world and forfeiting the soul.

column5: godliness benefits present and coming life
column6: The commentary says benefit reaches the hereafter, which is better and more lasting than worldly life; Paul says godliness has value for both present life and the life to come.

column5: teachings nourish those who receive them
column6: The commentary says a reminder is a means that nourishes and leads to good; Paul describes a good servant as nourished by the words of faith and sound teaching set before the community.

column5: invite the poor, disabled, and blind
column6: The commentary describes the blind seeker being neglected while attention goes to a socially prominent person; Jesus tells a host to invite the poor, crippled, lame, and blind, reversing that priority.

column5: benefit given to guests who cannot repay
column6: The commentary says benefit is not personal profit and may be hidden until the hereafter; Jesus blesses hospitality to those unable to repay, promising recompense at the resurrection of the righteous.

column5: rich guest honored while poor guest is shamed
column6: The commentary's Abasa example condemns favoring the prominent over a blind seeker; James describes an assembly giving a rich visitor a good seat and telling the poor visitor to stand or sit low.

column5: God chooses the poor rich in faith
column6: The commentary says the outwardly overlooked person may be the one who receives reminder; James says God chose the poor in the world's eyes to be rich in faith and heirs of the kingdom.

column5: Jesus calls the blind beggar the crowd rebuked
column6: The commentary's blind petitioner is initially ignored while the prominent man gets attention; Mark's crowd first silences Bartimaeus, but Jesus calls him forward, reversing who receives the messenger's attention.

column5: blind man receives sight and follows
column6: The commentary warns that outward appearance cannot reveal who will benefit from reminder; Jesus tells Bartimaeus his faith has saved him, and the healed man follows, making the overlooked hearer's response visible.

column5: blind beggar persists despite being silenced
column6: The commentary recounts a blind seeker ignored by the socially prominent; Luke's crowd rebukes a blind beggar for crying out, but he persists and Jesus stops to hear him.

column5: faith brings sight and salvation
column6: The commentary says the one assumed unlikely to benefit may be the one who receives; Jesus restores the beggar's sight and says his faith has saved him.

column5: those who do not see may see, and claimants to sight may be blind
column6: The commentary warns against judging a listener by outward status; after healing a blind man, Jesus describes a reversal in which the blind see and those claiming sight are exposed.

column5: claiming sight leaves guilt in place
column6: The commentary says outward certainty cannot disclose the hidden heart; Jesus tells the leaders that their claim to see leaves their sin, contrasting them with the formerly blind man who receives sight.

column5: Jerusalem refuses a gathering it was offered
column6: The commentary distinguishes an offered reminder from a hearer's refusal; Jesus says he longed to gather Jerusalem's children, but they were unwilling, a concrete image of rejected care without coercion.

column5: Paul did not shrink from declaring God's counsel
column6: The commentary's Sabbath admonishers warn so they can answer before God even if others do not benefit; Paul says he is innocent of everyone's blood because he did not withhold the whole counsel of God.

column5: Paul declares himself clear of bloodguilt
column6: The commentary frames warning as the admonisher's duty before God; Paul tells the elders he is innocent of the blood of all, the result of fully discharging that warning duty in the surrounding speech.

column5: covenant memory read through Jesus' birth
column6: The commentary reads Abraham and Moses' pages as the earlier source of a present reminder; Zechariah's inspired song interprets John's and Jesus' coming as God's remembrance of the covenant with the fathers.

column5: Hebrew cognate in a creation hymn
column6: The commentary says creation is publicly visible and functions as reminder; Psalm 19 celebrates the heavens proclaiming divine glory, a thematic companion in which creation itself testifies.

column5: consider one another and stir up good works
column6: The commentary says reminder's benefit reaches good action and worship; Hebrews asks believers to attend to one another so they may provoke love and good works, a communal application of exhortation.

column5: answer with gentleness and reverence
column6: The commentary connects the reminder to gentle speech and rejects coercive mastery; Peter tells believers to explain their hope with gentleness and reverence, a related Christian ethic of witness.
